author: Jimi Hendrix
text: When the power of love becomes stronger than the love of power, we will have peace.
suggested_reattribution: Sri Chinmoy (earliest confirmed print, 1971); possibly William Gladstone or William Ellery Channing for an earlier conceptual antecedent
notes: This quote is almost certainly not original to Jimi Hendrix. Goodreads tags it explicitly as 'misattributed' and cross-references 'william-gladstone.' Wikiquote's Sri Chinmoy article contains the note that 'a similar statement has also become attributed to Jimi Hendrix, though he could have been quoting or paraphrasing Chinmoy, or conceivably Gladstone.' Sri Chinmoy's 'My Rose Petals' (1971) is the earliest confirmed print citation: 'World Peace can be achieved when the Power Of Love replaces the Love Of Power.' William Gladstone is cited in 'The Forbes Book of Business Quotations' (1997) and in 'The National Elementary School Principal' (Vol. 28, 1948) with a very similar phrasing. An even earlier origin attributed to William Ellery Channing (1780–1842) circulates but is unverified. The exact phrasing in this record ('becomes stronger than' rather than 'overcomes') is a further variant. No primary Hendrix source (interview, recording, written statement) has ever been established. Misattribution to Hendrix is well-documented. | Suggested reattribution: Sri Chinmoy (earliest confirmed print, 1971); possibly William Gladstone or William Ellery Channing for an earlier conceptual antecedent

author: Abraham Lincoln
text: The best way to destroy an enemy is to make him a friend.
notes: Quote Investigator (quoteinvestigator.com/2020/05/13/make-friends/) investigated this thoroughly and concluded: 'based on current evidence this anecdote is apocryphal.' The saying has been attributed to Abraham Lincoln (via a post-mortem Civil War anecdote), Holy Roman Emperor Sigismund (d. 1437), and Mark Twain — all attributions appearing long after each figure's death. An 1867 New Orleans newspaper attributed a similar saying to Sigismund; the Lincoln anecdote form emerged by the 1940s. An 1858 Wisconsin newspaper cited the concept in relation to Cardinal Richelieu. An 1885 Vermont newspaper printed a similar line with no attribution. No primary Lincoln source (speech, letter, diary) has ever been found. The attribution to Lincoln is not credible.

author: Steve Jobs
text: The ones who are crazy enough to think that they can change the world are the ones who do.
suggested_reattribution: Apple "Think Different" campaign copy (TBWA\Chiat\Day — Rob Siltanen, Lee Clow, Craig Tanimoto), 1997
notes: This is the closing line of the Apple "Think Different" ad copy (1997), not a Jobs original. The copy was written at TBWA\Chiat\Day; creative director Rob Siltanen has publicly claimed principal authorship (with Lee Clow and Craig Tanimoto involved), and Jobs's role was as client, editor, and narrator of the unaired version he recorded. Because Jobs voiced it, it is universally credited to him. The ad wording is "the ones who are crazy enough to think they can change the world, are the ones who do" — the quoted text inserts "that." Attribution to Jobs as author is weak; my confidence in the ad-copy origin is high, but the individual copywriter credit is contested, so the reattribution below names the campaign rather than one person. | Suggested reattribution: Apple "Think Different" campaign copy (TBWA\Chiat\Day — Rob Siltanen, Lee Clow, Craig Tanimoto), 1997

author: Aristotle
text: We are what we repeatedly do. Excellence, then, is not an act, but a habit.
suggested_reattribution: Will Durant, The Story of Philosophy (1926), paraphrasing Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics
notes: The pre-flag is correct and this is one of the best-documented misattributions in circulation. The sentence is Will Durant's own summarizing gloss on the Nicomachean Ethics (roughly 1103a-b, on virtue as hexis acquired by habituation), written in The Story of Philosophy (1926). Aristotle never wrote it; Durant's line is set immediately after his paraphrase of Aristotle and the quotation marks migrated over time. Wikiquote lists it under Aristotle's misattributed section. Recommend crediting Durant and, if the Aristotelian idea is wanted, citing Nicomachean Ethics directly instead. | Suggested reattribution: Will Durant, The Story of Philosophy (1926), paraphrasing Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics

author: Pablo Picasso
text: The meaning of life is to find your gift. The purpose of life is to give it away.
suggested_reattribution: David Viscott, Finding Your Strength in Difficult Times (1993)
notes: No evidence Picasso ever said or wrote this, and it does not appear in his documented statements on art. The traceable origin is psychiatrist and broadcaster David Viscott, whose 1993 meditation book contains the line in the form "The purpose of life is to discover your gift. The meaning of life is to give your gift away." Note that the popular Picasso version swaps "meaning" and "purpose" relative to Viscott's original — a signature of a quote that has been passed along orally rather than copied from a text. Attribution to Picasso should be treated as false. | Suggested reattribution: David Viscott, Finding Your Strength in Difficult Times (1993)

author: Hafiz
text: Start seeing everything as god, but keep it a secret.
notes: This is a Daniel Ladinsky line, not Hafez. Ladinsky's popular 'Hafiz' volumes (The Gift; I Heard God Laughing) are his own original poems, not translations — he has said in his own prefaces that they came to him rather than from the Persian text, and scholars of Persian literature (and Wikiquote's Hafez page) treat the whole Ladinsky corpus as unattributable to Hafez. This aphorism's compressed, modern-English epigram form is unlike any authentic ghazal line. I did not attempt to name which Ladinsky volume it appears in, since I am not certain. | Suggested reattribution: Daniel Ladinsky

author: Alan Watts
text: Your soul is not in your body. Your body is in your soul.
notes: This formulation is classically Meister Eckhart's ('the soul is not in the body; the body is in the soul'), and the underlying doctrine is Plotinian — the Enneads argue expressly that the body is in the soul rather than the soul in the body. Watts read and quoted Eckhart constantly, so he may well have said this in a lecture, but he would have been relaying it, not coining it. Attributing it to Watts as author is likely wrong. My confidence in Eckhart as the formulator is moderate rather than high, hence the hedge. | Suggested reattribution: Meister Eckhart (idea originating with Plotinus)

author: Anonymous
text: If you want to see the brave, look at those who can forgive. If you want to see the heroic, look at those who can love in return for hatred.
suggested_reattribution: Bhagavad Gita (conventional attribution; appears to be a loose paraphrase, not a verse translation)
notes: The record's author field is 'Anonymous', which is defensible but incomplete: this passage circulates very widely as Bhagavad Gita, and the record's own context tag ('Hindu, Krishna-consciousness') points the same way. It is not a literal translation of any verse I can identify — it reads as a loose devotional paraphrase in the manner of popular English Gita anthologies rather than of Sanskrit rendered line by line. So 'Bhagavad Gita' would be the conventional attribution, but a real verse anchor is exactly what I cannot supply. | Suggested reattribution: Bhagavad Gita (conventional attribution; appears to be a loose paraphrase, not a verse translation)
